title: Transient ischaemic attack (TIA)
subject: neurology
summary: Treat every suspected TIA as a stroke warning: aspirin immediately, same-day brain and vessel imaging and ECG, and aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days for high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor stroke, started within 24 hours.

sections.title: Recognise
items: TIA: transient focal neurological dysfunction caused by ischaemia without acute infarction on imaging. Most episodes last under 1 hour. A persisting deficit is a stroke: activate the stroke pathway.
Typical symptoms: unilateral weakness or numbness, speech disturbance, transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax), hemianopia, or ataxia with other brainstem signs.
Mimics: hypoglycaemia (check glucose), migraine aura (spreading, positive symptoms), focal seizure, syncope, transient global amnesia, isolated vertigo.
Risk is front-loaded: 90-day stroke risk can reach about 18%, with almost half of those strokes in the first 2 days.

sections.title: Immediate actions
items: Give aspirin 300 mg orally immediately unless contraindicated (NICE). If anticoagulated, bleeding risk is high or haemorrhage is suspected, image the brain first.
Arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset. If discharged from the ED, neurology or stroke follow-up within 48 hours and no later than 1 week (AHA 2023).

ABCD2 score (max 7): age 60 or more (1); BP 140/90 mmHg or more (1); unilateral weakness (2) or speech disturbance without weakness (1); duration 60 minutes or more (2) or 10 to 59 minutes (1); diabetes (1). A score of 4 or more defines high-risk TIA for DAPT.
ABCD2 limits: it misses high-risk causes such as AF, carotid stenosis and DWI-positive lesions. NICE advises not to use ABCD2 to set urgency; use it mainly to select DAPT eligibility.
Admit or assess the same day: crescendo TIAs (2 or more in a week), known or new AF, symptomatic carotid stenosis, DWI lesion, diagnostic uncertainty, or when investigations cannot be done quickly.

sections.title: Investigations (same day)
items: Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted and blood-sensitive sequences is preferred; use CT if MRI is unavailable, to exclude haemorrhage and mimics.
Vascular imaging without delay: CT or MR angiography of head and neck, or carotid Doppler for anterior circulation events.
12-lead ECG and cardiac rhythm monitoring; prolonged monitoring if no cause is found. Echocardiography when cardioembolism is suspected.
Bloods: CBC, glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, electrolytes, creatinine, coagulation. ESR and CRP if age over 50 with transient monocular loss (giant cell arteritis).

sections.title: Antiplatelet therapy
items: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor stroke (NIHSS 3 or less), non-cardioembolic: aspirin plus clopidogrel started ideally within 12 to 24 hours (at least within 7 days), continued for 21 days, then a single antiplatelet (AHA/ASA 2021).
Loading: clopidogrel 300 to 600 mg plus aspirin 300 mg (if not already given), then clopidogrel 75 mg plus aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily for 21 days.
Presumed large artery atherosclerosis (stenosis 50% or more) with ABCD2 4 or more or NIHSS 5 or less presenting at 24 to 72 hours: 21 days of DAPT is still reasonable (AHA/ASA 2026).

Alternative: ticagrelor 180 mg loading then 90 mg twice daily with aspirin for 30 days (NIHSS 5 or less or ABCD2 6 or more), or for 21 days in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers, who are common in South Asians. More bleeding than aspirin alone.
Do not continue DAPT beyond 90 days. Long term: clopidogrel 75 mg daily or aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily.

sections.title: Cause-specific prevention
items: Atrial fibrillation: oral anticoagulation (DOAC preferred) instead of antiplatelets, started promptly once haemorrhage is excluded; do not add antiplatelets routinely.
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70 to 99% (NICE also 50 to 99% by NASCET): carotid endarterectomy or stenting within 2 weeks when perioperative risk is below 6%.
Symptomatic intracranial stenosis 70 to 99%: aspirin plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days with intensive risk factor control.
High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg daily), aiming for LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L).
BP target below 130/80 mmHg for most patients after the acute phase; HbA1c 7% or less for most people with diabetes; stop smoking; limit alcohol; regular exercise.

sections.title: Disposition and advice
items: ED discharge is reasonable only when brain and vessel imaging and ECG are done, the deficit has fully resolved, antiplatelets are started and specialist review is booked within 48 hours.
Tell the patient to call an ambulance immediately for any new symptom: a stroke may still be treatable with thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
Driving: advise no driving until assessed and follow local law (UK DVLA car licence: no driving for 1 month after a TIA; 1 month after each episode if recurrent).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Being reassured by a low ABCD2 score in a patient with AF, carotid stenosis or a DWI lesion.
Using DAPT for cardioembolic TIA instead of anticoagulation, or continuing DAPT long term.
Delaying carotid imaging: the benefit of endarterectomy falls sharply after 2 weeks.
Labelling isolated vertigo, syncope or confusion as TIA without considering alternatives, or dismissing transient monocular blindness.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.dose: 300 mg orally immediately, then 75 to 100 mg daily with clopidogrel for 21 days
drugs.notes: Long term 75 to 150 mg daily if chosen as single antiplatelet.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.dose: 300 to 600 mg orally loading, then 75 mg daily
drugs.notes: With aspirin for 21 days in high-risk TIA or minor stroke, then continue alone.

drugs.name: Ticagrelor
drugs.dose: 180 mg orally loading, then 90 mg twice daily (with aspirin) for 21 to 30 days
drugs.notes: Alternative to clopidogrel, including CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers. Higher bleeding risk.
